The time of the onset of Antarctic continental glaciation and related climatic changes are matters of some disagreement, and the details of the history of the Antarctic Ice Sheet are unknown. The times and magnitudes of waxing and waning of the ice sheet, and the relationship of these events to surges, are yet to be established.
Studies of the particulate matter, especially terrestrial volcanic dust, will provide insight into the history of volcanic activity, a matter of interest not only to geologists but also meteorologists and glaciologists. Of significance also is the study of the variation of atmospheric chemistry as recorded in the snow stratigraphy. These ice cores will be carefully analyzed for evidences of pollutants from the atmosphere and should provide additional insight into the changes of the amounts through time.
The study of the components of the water column beneath the Ross Ice Shelf is of equal importance. The formation of the cold and saline waters found on the continental shelf below the Ross Sea may occur beneath the ice shelf. It is suspected that these shelf waters lead eventually to the production of Antarctic bottom water, a water mass which has an important effect on the world's oceans. The complex interaction between sea water and the shelf ice, and the exchange of water from beneath the ice shelf with the open sea, is not well known. The ice cores should provide evidence for or against the possible accretion of sea ice onto the bottom of the Ross Ice Shelf.
